titleText.en: Saying 'what kind of an idiot doesn't know about the Yellowstone supervolcano' is so much more boring than telling someone about the Yellowstone supervolcano for the first time.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive's title attribute is preserved exactly as its truncated value, including the trailing space; the official English title attribute is complete. Vision read SI as I, ESTOY as STOY, OPORTUNIDAD as CPORTUNIDAD, split OSTRAS, missed Y in the product question, lost the accent in SÚPER, and severely misread the two lower-left infographic labels. The country names, product names, percentages, and Arabic-numeral quantities are audited exclusions; chart operators and punctuation are artwork or ordinary punctuation.

regions.labelEs: INTENTO NO BURLARME DE LA GENTE QUE ADMITE QUE NO CONOCE ALGO.

applications.explanationEn: Intento supplies the trying action, and burlarme remains an infinitive despite the intervening negation.
Me attaches to the infinitive burlar and marks the speaker within the pronominal verb.
Burlarme carries the matching pronoun, de is required by the verb, and la gente supplies the target.
Que links gente to the description supplied by admite.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone tries to do an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of intentar followed directly by the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: No linking preposition is needed between the two verbs. Intento abrir means “I try to open,” and intentamos salir means “we try to leave.” The attempted action stays in its basic -ar, -er, or -ir form.

example.en: We try to open the window.

cards.answerEn: to make fun; to mock (with myself as the actor)
cards.noteEn: Burlarme combines burlar with attached me. In burlarse de, the attached pronoun marks the person doing the mocking, while de introduces the target.

example.en: I try not to make fun of anyone.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

example.en: I want to help you.

cards.questionEn: How do you express making fun of a person or thing?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching pronominal form of burlarse followed by de and the target.
cards.noteEn: The pronoun changes with the subject: me burlo, te burlas, se burla, and so on. De remains before what is mocked.

example.es: No debemos burlarnos de los demás.
example.en: We should not make fun of others.

cards.questionEn: Why does the comic treat an apparently obvious fact as a daily opportunity?
cards.answerEn: Because people continually reach the age at which they can encounter any familiar fact for the first time, so sharing it can be more enjoyable than mocking them for not already knowing it.
cards.noteEn: The comic estimates that roughly 1,300 people in Spain encounter a given piece of common knowledge for the first time each day. The product demonstration turns the calculation into a concrete moment of delighted discovery.

cards.answerEn: of; required after burlarse before the target
cards.noteEn: Burlarse uses de before the person or thing being mocked. Natural English normally expresses the whole pattern as ‘make fun of’ or ‘mock.’

example.es: No te burles de tu hermano.
example.en: Do not make fun of your brother.

cards.questionEn: How do you add information about a named person or thing using “who,” “that,” or “which”?
cards.answerEn: Put que after the person or thing, then add a verb and the information about it.
cards.noteEn: Que links the added description to the person or thing before it. It does not change for masculine, feminine, singular, or plural nouns. The added part needs a verb: la casa que vimos means “the house that we saw.”

example.es: La casa que vimos es azul.
example.en: The house that we saw is blue.

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.noteEn: Admite is the present form of admitir for one person or thing. A following que clause states what is acknowledged.

example.es: El autor admite que se equivocó.
example.en: The author admits that he was wrong.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: knows; is familiar with (a fact or subject)
cards.noteEn: Conocer often means being acquainted with a person, place, subject, or item of knowledge. It contrasts with saber used for knowing that a statement is true.

example.en: She knows the subject well.

cards.noteEn: Por can introduce the unit used to divide or distribute a quantity. The unit after por stays singular when it means “for each one.”

example.en: There are two books per student.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “everyone” or “everybody”?
cards.noteEn: The words literally resemble “all the world,” but this fixed expression refers to all people in the relevant group. Grammatically it is singular, so a following present-time verb uses a singular form: todo el mundo sabe, not saben.

example.es: Todo el mundo sabe la respuesta.
example.en: Everyone knows the answer.

cards.noteEn: Sabe is the present form of saber for one person or thing. It expresses knowledge of information; before an infinitive it can instead mean ‘knows how to.’

example.es: Todo el mundo sabe la respuesta.
example.en: Everyone knows the answer.

cards.answerEn: Use al followed by the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Al + verb tells when the main action happens. Translate it naturally as “when,” “on,” or “upon”: al llegar means “when arriving” or simply “when someone arrives.”
cards.questionEn: How do you say “when doing something” or “upon doing something”?

example.en: When I arrive, I will call you.

cards.answerEn: to reach; to arrive at (a life stage)
cards.noteEn: Llegar keeps its ordinary arrival sense when a following a phrase names an age or stage, as in llegar a adulto or llegar a los treinta.

example.es: Al llegar a adulta, se mudó.
example.en: When she reached adulthood, she moved.

cards.answerEn: to; introduces the endpoint of a change

cards.noteEn: Adultos can name adult men or a mixed group of adults. The feminine plural is adultas.

example.en: The activity is for adults.

cards.noteEn: De is fixed with media in the statistical expression de media. Its meaning comes from the complete expression rather than the usual possession or origin senses.

example.en: Ten messages arrive on average.

cards.questionEn: How do you state that a number is an average?
cards.answerEn: Use de media after the measured quantity or statement.
cards.noteEn: De media is a compact statistical expression meaning ‘on average.’

example.es: La clase dura cincuenta minutos de media.
example.en: The class lasts fifty minutes on average.

cards.noteEn: Media is the feminine noun for an average. In de media it describes a typical value across many cases.

example.es: La media es de ocho horas.
example.en: The average is eight hours.

cards.noteEn: In a frequency expression, al combines a + el before a masculine time period: una vez al mes means ‘once per month.’

example.es: Voy al médico dos veces al año.
example.en: I go to the doctor twice a year.

cards.promptEs: lo, la, los, las delante de un verbo conjugado
cards.questionEn: Where do you put the Spanish word for “it” or “them” when the main verb already shows who acts and when?
cards.answerEn: Put lo, la, los, or las directly before that verb.
cards.noteEn: These short words replace the person or thing directly affected by the action; that role is called the direct object. Choose lo or los for a masculine thing, la or las for a feminine thing, and match singular or plural. Before a verb form such as conté or vimos, write the short word separately in front: lo conté, las vimos. With an unchanged dictionary form, it can instead attach to the end, as in verlo.

example.en: The movie—we watched it yesterday.

cards.answerEn: they are (helping to describe an action in progress)
cards.noteEn: Here están is the plural form of estar used before an action ending in -ando or -iendo.

example.en: They are cooking.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by an action word ending in -ando or -iendo.
cards.noteEn: Estar changes to show who is doing the action: estoy, estás, está, and so on. For most verbs, replace -ar with -ando (hablar → hablando) and replace -er or -ir with -iendo (comer → comiendo, vivir → viviendo). This is similar to English “am/is/are doing.”
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is in the middle of doing something?

example.en: I am reading.

cards.noteEn: Escuchando is the ongoing-action form of escuchar. It follows a form of estar to describe listening or hearing in progress.

example.en: They are hearing the news.

cards.answerEn: for; begins por primera vez, ‘for the first time’
cards.noteEn: Por is fixed with primera vez in this time expression. Its meaning comes from the complete expression rather than a price, cause, path, or per-unit use.

example.en: We visited Granada for the first time.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something happens for the first time?
cards.noteEn: Primera agrees with the understood feminine noun vez. The three words work together as a time expression.

example.es: Probó el mango por primera vez.
example.en: She tried mango for the first time.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of enterarse
cards.noteEn: Enterarse is a pronominal verb meaning to find out or learn some information. Se changes with the subject and stays beside the changed verb or attaches to an infinitive.

example.en: She found out yesterday.

cards.noteEn: Enteró is the completed-past form used with se for one person: se enteró. The information learned can follow de or be understood from context.

example.es: Carlos se enteró de la reunión.
example.en: Carlos found out about the meeting.

cards.noteEn: Nacer is the dictionary form for coming into life. Spanish commonly uses al nacer for ‘at birth’ or ‘when born.’

example.es: El bebé pesó tres kilos al nacer.
example.en: The baby weighed three kilos at birth.

cards.noteEn: Lo replaces a masculine singular thing, or sometimes a whole idea, as the direct object. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.

example.es: Tengo el libro y lo leo.
example.en: I have the book and I’m reading it.

cards.noteEn: Tasa is a feminine noun for a rate, especially a quantity measured relative to a population or period.

example.en: The employment rate increased.

cards.questionEn: How do you name the rate of births in a population?
cards.noteEn: The phrase is a demographic measure, often stated per year or per thousand inhabitants.

example.es: La tasa de natalidad varía por región.
example.en: The birth rate varies by region.

cards.answerEn: often no separate English word; links a noun to another noun that names its type or use
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between two nouns where English uses a noun directly before another noun. For example, una taza de café is ‘a coffee cup,’ and material de oficina is ‘office material.’

example.en: I need a coffee cup.

cards.answerEn: birth rate; births in a population
cards.noteEn: Natalidad refers to births considered as a demographic measure. Tasa de natalidad is the standard expression for a birth rate.

example.en: The birth rate fell this year.

cards.questionEn: How do you introduce a real or possible condition with “if”?
cards.answerEn: Use si without an accent, followed by an ordinary present-time verb form.
cards.noteEn: This pattern treats the condition as genuinely possible. Spanish normally does not put a future-tense verb directly after si in this kind of condition; the result can appear separately as a statement, prediction, or command.

example.en: If you have time, call.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; marks an “I” verb that is used with me
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs conventionally come with me, te, se, nos, or os even when no one literally acts on themselves. Me marks the speaker's form. English usually absorbs it into the verb's meaning.

example.en: I complain about the noise.

cards.noteEn: Burlo is the present yo form used in me burlo de. Me marks the speaker as the actor in the pronominal expression, and de introduces the target.

example.es: No me burlo de sus preguntas.
example.en: I do not make fun of their questions.

cards.answerEn: them (masculine or mixed group, after a preposition)
cards.noteEn: Ellos usually means ‘they,’ but after a preposition such as con, para, or sin, English uses ‘them.’

example.en: I am going with them.

cards.noteEn: Some speakers use les for a masculine or mixed plural group as the direct object. More widely taught standard usage would normally use los here; les is standard when the people are indirect recipients.

example.es: A esos alumnos les vi ayer.
example.en: I saw those students yesterday.

cards.answerEn: so that (before que and a desired result)
cards.noteEn: Before que and a full event, para introduces the purpose of an action. Translate para que together as ‘so that’ or ‘in order that.’

example.es: Hablo despacio para que todos entiendan.
example.en: I speak slowly so that everyone understands.

cards.questionEn: How do you express a purpose when someone or something else carries out the desired result?
cards.answerEn: Use para que, then put the result verb in the special form used for a purpose that is not yet a fact.
cards.noteEn: That special form is called the subjunctive. It appears because the second action is intended or desired, not presented as an established fact. For example, ordinary ve becomes vea, and ordinary viene becomes venga. Use para plus an unchanged action verb instead when the same person performs both actions.

example.es: Dejo una nota para que Ana la vea.
example.en: I leave a note so that Ana sees it.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes para que, ‘so that’
cards.noteEn: Que completes the purpose connector para que before an event with its own person or thing carrying out the action.

example.es: Cierra la puerta para que no entre frío.
example.en: Close the door so that cold air does not come in.

cards.promptEs: cuando + presente de subjuntivo para un hecho futuro
cards.questionEn: After cuando, how do you describe an event that has not happened yet?
cards.answerEn: Use cuando followed by a present subjunctive form for the future event; put the main result in an ordinary future or command form.
cards.noteEn: The subjunctive is a special verb form used here because the time of the future event is not yet a fact. For example, mover changes to mueva. Spanish does not normally put a future-tense form immediately after cuando in this pattern.

example.en: I will call you when I arrive.

cards.answerEn: they have (special form after a future cuando)
cards.noteEn: Tengan is a special form of tener used after cuando when the event is still expected or hypothetical rather than presented as an established fact.

example.en: Call me when they have time.

cards.noteEn: Momentos is the plural of momento. It can refer to short stretches of time or particular occasions and situations.

example.en: We all have difficult moments.

cards.questionEn: Why can a Spanish sentence contain both no and another negative word?
cards.answerEn: When the second negative word follows the verb, keep no before the verb too.
cards.noteEn: Spanish commonly uses matching negative words together. No tiene ninguna means “it does not have any”; it does not become a positive meaning as two negatives sometimes do in formal English.

example.en: I do not have any doubt.

cards.answerEn: they tell; they recount (special form in a desired result)
cards.noteEn: Cuenten is a special form of contar. It appears after para que when the telling is the desired or prevented result.

example.es: Habla bajo para que no cuenten el secreto.
example.en: Speak quietly so that they do not tell the secret.

cards.noteEn: After a negative verb, nada is commonly translated as “anything,” even though its basic meaning is “nothing.” Spanish keeps both negative words.

example.en: I don’t see anything.

cards.noteEn: Pierdo is the present yo form of perder. With oportunidad it means missing or losing an opportunity.

example.es: Pierdo una oportunidad si no voy.
example.en: I miss an opportunity if I do not go.

cards.answerEn: Use para followed by the verb’s dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Use para + verb when the same person or thing performs both actions: in estudio para aprender, I both study and learn. When someone else performs the second action, Spanish needs the different pattern para que.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “in order to do something” in Spanish?

example.en: I study in order to learn.

cards.answerEn: to have it; in pasarlo bien, to have a good time
cards.noteEn: Pasarlo combines pasar with attached lo. In the fixed expression pasarlo bien, the two words describe enjoying oneself rather than physically passing an object.

example.en: We want to have a good time.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone has or wants to have a good time?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of pasar with lo and bien; in an infinitive, use pasarlo bien.
cards.noteEn: The expression is fixed: lo normally stands before a changed form, as in lo pasamos bien, but attaches to the infinitive pasar.

example.en: I hope you all have a good time.

cards.answerEn: well; completes pasarlo bien, ‘have a good time’
cards.noteEn: Bien completes the fixed expression pasarlo bien. Its meaning belongs to the whole enjoyment expression rather than an evaluation of how a task was performed.

example.es: Lo pasamos bien en la fiesta.
example.en: We had a good time at the party.

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?

example.en: What is your name?

cards.answerEn: is; belongs to the stated category
cards.noteEn: Es is the present form of ser used for one person or thing. Between two naming words, it identifies or classifies the first as the second.

example.en: Chess is a game.

cards.noteEn: Ostras is a mild informal exclamation of surprise. Its literal noun meaning is ‘oysters,’ but no oysters are meant in this reaction.

example.en: Wow, what a surprise!

cards.noteEn: Venga is a form of venir, but speakers also use it by itself to urge or encourage someone. In that use it does not literally tell the listener to come to a place.

example.en: Come on, team, we can do it!

cards.noteEn: Vamos is the “we” form of ir, “to go.” Speakers also use it to propose that the group go somewhere or begin moving.

example.en: Let's go to the park.

cards.noteEn: Al is the required contraction of a + el. Spanish writes them as one word whenever both occur together.

example.en: I’m going to the market.

cards.noteEn: Súper is an informal shortened noun for supermercado. The written accent distinguishes its stressed pronunciation.

example.en: I am going to the supermarket for milk.

cards.answerEn: why?; for what reason? (with qué left understood)
cards.noteEn: In the short echo ¿por?, the usual qué is omitted because the question being repeated is already clear.

example.en: “We have to leave.” “Why?”

cards.promptEs: ser para identidad · estar para ubicación
cards.questionEn: Which Spanish “to be” verb says what something is, and which says where it is?
cards.answerEn: Use ser for identity or a defining description; use estar for the location of a person or thing.
cards.noteEn: This contrast is not simply permanent versus temporary. Forms of ser such as soy and es identify or describe what something is. Forms of estar such as están normally locate people and things. Events are a common exception: Spanish uses ser to say where or when an event takes place.

example.es: El museo es famoso y está en Madrid.
example.en: The museum is famous and is in Madrid.

cards.noteEn: Una can stand on its own for one feminine person or thing when the noun is already understood. It is not introducing a new noun in this use.

example.en: I want one that is comfortable.

cards.questionEn: How do you identify one member of a larger group?
cards.answerEn: Use uno or una, then de, then name the plural group.
cards.noteEn: Choose uno or una to match the understood member. A demonstrative or article may appear before the plural group: uno de esos libros, una de las profesoras.

example.es: Ella es una de las mejores jugadoras.
example.en: She is one of the best players.

cards.answerEn: of; links one member to a larger group
cards.noteEn: After uno or una, de introduces the group that the one member belongs to.

example.en: He is one of my neighbors.

cards.noteEn: Afortunados can be a masculine or mixed plural adjective or a noun for fortunate people.

example.en: The lucky ones received tickets.
